body:
What makes a heat wave dangerous?

A heat wave is a period of abnormally hot weather identified using meteorological criteria. Its public-health importance lies in the body's difficulty in losing excess heat, particularly during prolonged exposure or physical work.

Heat stress can develop when the body gains or produces more heat than it can release. High air temperature, humidity, direct sunshine, insufficient drinking water, inadequate rest and strenuous activity can all increase danger. Humidity is especially important because it reduces the effectiveness of sweat evaporation, a major means of cooling the body.

In Gujarat, heat exposure is relevant to outdoor workers, construction labourers, farmers, traffic personnel, street vendors, industrial workers and people living in poorly ventilated housing. Older persons, infants, pregnant women and people with certain medical conditions may require additional protection.

IMD heat-wave criteria

IMD uses maximum air temperature together with departures from normal and other conditions to describe heat-wave events. The following figures are useful for distinguishing meteorological categories from health effects.

IMD criterionTemperature conditionMeaning
Consideration for plainsMaximum temperature at least 40°CBasic temperature condition for heat-wave classification
Consideration for coastal stationsMaximum at least 37°C and departure at least 4.5°CCoastal heat-wave criterion
Departure-based heat wave4.5°C to 6.4°C above normalHeat-wave range under the departure criterion
Departure-based severe heat waveMore than 6.4°C above normalSevere heat-wave range under the departure criterion
Actual-temperature criterion for plains onlyAt least 45°C for heat wave; at least 47°C for severe heat waveAlternative actual-maximum-temperature thresholds

For an official heat-wave declaration in a meteorological subdivision, the applicable criteria must be met at 2 or more stations for at least 2 consecutive days, with declaration on the second day. Therefore, an isolated temperature reading does not necessarily mean that an official subdivision-wide declaration has been made.

Heat illness can occur even when a location does not satisfy IMD's formal heat-wave criteria. The meteorological classification describes weather conditions; it is not a medical test of whether an individual is safe.

Heat exhaustion and heat stroke

Heat exhaustion may involve heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or unusual tiredness. The affected person should stop exertion, move to a cooler place and receive appropriate assistance.

Heat stroke is a medical emergency in which the body's temperature regulation fails and serious illness develops. Confusion, altered consciousness, collapse or seizures during heat exposure are danger signs. Emergency medical help and prompt cooling are essential. A person with impaired consciousness should not be forced to drink.

Ahmedabad's Heat Action Plan

Ahmedabad provides an important Gujarat example of city-level preparedness. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation launched its Heat Action Plan in 2013, establishing a comprehensive system for heat warnings and public-health preparedness. Its approach included public awareness, training for health and community workers, early warning and coordination between agencies.

A Heat Action Plan connects weather forecasts with measures that reduce illness and death. It identifies vulnerable groups, communicates preventive advice, strengthens health-system readiness and encourages arrangements for drinking water, shade and cooling.

Standard public precautions

  • Drink sufficient safe water and avoid unnecessary exposure during the hottest hours.
  • Use shade, cool indoor spaces and suitable light clothing.
  • Reduce strenuous outdoor activity when possible and provide rest breaks for exposed workers.
  • Check on older people, infants and others who may not recognise or communicate heat distress.
  • Seek medical help promptly when serious heat-related symptoms appear.

Local action plans should respond to actual weather forecasts and the needs of the population rather than relying on a single temperature figure for all locations.

Prelims focus

  • IMD's basic plains temperature condition for heat-wave consideration is 40°C.
  • For coastal stations, a maximum of at least 37°C and departure of at least 4.5°C are relevant.
  • A departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C indicates the departure-based heat-wave range.
  • Ahmedabad launched its pioneering Heat Action Plan in 2013.
  • Heat stroke with altered consciousness is a medical emergency.
  • Trap: Formal IMD heat-wave criteria are not the minimum temperatures at which heat illness can occur.

[Sources: India Meteorological Department, Meteorological Olympiad Study Material, section on Heat Wave Criteria, consulted 2 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation Heat Action Plan, launched 2013; Natural Resources Defense Council, Indian City Launches First-Ever Heat Wave Preparation and Warning System, 16 April 2013.]

body:
Why a coordinated approach is necessary

Cyclones, droughts, floods, heat waves and industrial accidents require different immediate precautions, but they depend on several common capacities: reliable information, clear public warnings, prepared local institutions, accessible shelters or support services, and continuity of essential supplies.

Integrated disaster planning means that departments and communities plan together while retaining hazard-specific actions. For example, a cyclone plan may require coastal evacuation; a drought plan prioritises water security; a heat plan concentrates on reducing exposure and preparing health services; and a chemical emergency plan may require either sheltering indoors or evacuation depending on the incident.

The basic institutional framework

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 establishes a framework for disaster management across India. At the national level, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) is chaired by the Prime Minister. State-level disaster-management authorities are ordinarily chaired by the Chief Minister. At the district level, the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) is chaired by the District Magistrate or Collector, with an elected representative of the local authority as ex officio co-chairperson. Where a Zila Parishad exists, its chairperson is co-chairperson; in Sixth Schedule tribal areas, the autonomous district council's Chief Executive Member is ex officio co-chairperson.

Gujarat established the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) on 8 February 2001 following the January 2001 earthquake. Gujarat also enacted the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003. The national law of 2005 subsequently provided the broader nationwide statutory framework.

InstitutionLevelCore responsibility
NDMANationalNational policy and direction for disaster management
GSDMAGujarat stateState planning, risk reduction and coordination
DDMADistrictDistrict planning and coordination of local disaster management
Municipal and panchayat institutionsLocalLocal preparedness, public services and community-level implementation
IMD and other technical agenciesTechnical forecastingProvide hazard observations and specialised warnings

Who forecasts, who decides and who acts?

A technically accurate forecast does not automatically tell every resident what action to take. Weather and flood-monitoring agencies provide specialised information. Disaster-management authorities interpret the information for their geographical area, assess the vulnerable population and coordinate protective decisions. Local institutions, emergency services, health departments and community organisations help communicate and implement those decisions.

Integrated district preparedness

District plans should identify multiple hazards and connect them with settlement locations, hospitals, transport routes, water supplies, electricity systems, schools and vulnerable groups. Essential requirements include:

  • Risk assessment: identify the hazards, exposed settlements and people needing additional assistance.
  • Early warning: establish who receives technical forecasts and how reliable messages reach communities.
  • Protective arrangements: identify shelters, safe evacuation routes and other hazard-appropriate precautions.
  • Essential services: plan for safe drinking water, food, health care, electricity and communication continuity.
  • Community participation: involve residents, schools, industries, local leaders and volunteers in awareness and preparedness.
  • Recovery planning: restore services and livelihoods while reducing the conditions that created serious vulnerability.

Plans are updated, not treated as permanent predictions

GSDMA's public plan catalogue, consulted on 2 November 2026, lists the State Disaster Management Plan for 2025–26 in 2 volumes and separate hazard-related plans. These are planning documents for the stated period; they are not forecasts of which disasters will occur during a particular year.

For example, an integrated district plan can recognise that intense coastal rainfall may cause urban flooding while a nearby industrial site also requires protective arrangements. Coordinated planning helps avoid conflicting warnings and ensures that the same road, shelter or water source is not assumed to be available for incompatible purposes.

Prelims focus

  • Disaster Management Act: 2005.
  • NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister.
  • The State Disaster Management Authority is ordinarily chaired by the Chief Minister.
  • DDMA is chaired by the District Magistrate or Collector.
  • GSDMA was established on 8 February 2001; Gujarat's state disaster-management legislation dates to 2003.
  • Trap: A forecasting agency supplies technical warnings, while district and local authorities coordinate protective action.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, provisions on national, state and district authorities; GSDMA, Chapter XIII, institutional history and disaster management arrangements; GSDMA, State Disaster Management Plan catalogue, 2025–26 Vols. I and II, status checked 2 November 2026; GSDMA, Disaster Management Plan at Other Levels, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Integrated Disaster Planning and Institutional Roles in Gujarat

body:
Why Gujarat needs industrial-disaster preparedness

Gujarat has large concentrations of chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, petroleum-processing and related industries. Such industries contribute substantially to production and employment, but they may involve hazardous substances whose accidental release, ignition or uncontrolled reaction can cause serious harm.

An industrial disaster is not simply the normal presence of industry or routine pollution. It involves an accident or other event causing or threatening substantial injury, loss of life, environmental damage or disruption. Not every industrial incident becomes a major disaster, and not every industrial facility presents the same level of risk.

Important industrial regions

GSDMA identifies an approximately 400 km industrial stretch from Ahmedabad to Vapi as Gujarat's Golden Corridor, noted for a high concentration of chemical industries. Ankleshwar in Bharuch district is a particularly significant chemical-industrial centre.

Other important examples include the Vapi industrial area in Valsad district, chemical-industrial areas around Vadodara, the Dahej petrochemical and port region in Bharuch, the Hazira industrial-port area near Surat, and petroleum-related facilities around Jamnagar. These examples illustrate different industrial concentrations rather than implying that all facilities handle the same hazardous substances.

Recognising the main accident types

HazardBasic meaningPossible consequences
Toxic releaseHazardous material unintentionally escapes into the environmentPoisoning, breathing difficulties or environmental contamination
FireCombustible material burns uncontrollablyBurn injuries, smoke exposure and property damage
ExplosionRapid energy release creates a damaging pressure effectBlast injuries, structural damage and secondary fires
Hazardous liquid spillDangerous material escapes from storage or transportContact exposure, contamination and possible fire risk
Transport accidentHazardous cargo is involved in an incident during movementEffects along roads, rail routes, pipelines or port facilities

The consequences depend on the substance involved, the quantity released, the weather, the surrounding population and the effectiveness of safety arrangements. A toxic release and a flammable-material accident may require different protective decisions.

Why ports require additional attention

Ports may handle petroleum products, chemicals and other hazardous cargo. A maritime industrial complex can contain vessels, loading facilities, storage areas, pipelines and transport connections. The accident risk is therefore not confined to a single factory building.

At coastal sites, a cyclone, heavy rainfall or storm surge may disrupt transport, flood access routes or damage supporting infrastructure. These conditions can complicate response to an industrial accident or, in some circumstances, contribute to a secondary incident.

When a natural hazard triggers a technological accident, the resulting sequence is often called a Natech event, meaning a natural-hazard-triggered technological accident. The basic lesson is that coastal and industrial disaster plans must consider their possible interaction.

Risk reduction and community preparedness

Safe industrial operations depend on compliance with applicable rules, suitable planning, inspection, worker training and clear emergency arrangements. At the community level, preparedness requires identifying nearby hazards, knowing official warning sources, understanding whether evacuation or indoor sheltering may be instructed, and recognising routes to designated safe places.

Local authorities should consider hospitals, schools, densely occupied neighbourhoods and other sensitive locations in planning around hazardous industrial installations. Public communication must be understandable and suitable for the particular hazard; a single instruction cannot safely cover every possible chemical accident.

Prelims focus

  • GSDMA describes the Ahmedabad–Vapi industrial stretch of about 400 km as the Golden Corridor.
  • Ankleshwar is in Bharuch district.
  • Dahej is an important industrial-port area of Bharuch; Hazira is associated with Surat.
  • Toxic release, fire, explosion and hazardous-material transport accidents are distinct industrial hazards.
  • A natural hazard can trigger a technological accident, producing a Natech event.
  • Trap: Routine industrial pollution and a sudden industrial disaster are related environmental concerns but are not identical concepts.

[Sources: GSDMA, State Chemical and Industrial Disaster Management Plan, Gujarat industrial-risk profile and Golden Corridor; GSDMA, Chapter XIII, section 13.12, Chemical and Industrial Disaster Management Plan; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, industrial-estate and Dahej development information; Gujarat Maritime Board, port information; sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
